hints: Think about which functional group containing nitrogen can gain hydrogen to become an $\text{NH}_2$ group attached directly to a benzene ring.
Recall the classic pair of reagents used to reduce an aromatic nitro compound, where a metal supplies electrons in acidic solution with heating.
walkthrough:
Spot the change from N with oxygen to N with hydrogen**
Picture $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$. The nitrogen is joined to the ring and to hydrogens only. To make that by reduction you need to start from a more oxidised nitrogen on the same ring. That is the nitro group, $\text{NO}_2$, so the starting material is nitrobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$.

Choose the reducing system for an aromatic nitro group**
Reduction of $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ needs a strong source of electrons plus $\text{H}^+$. Tin in concentrated hydrochloric acid does exactly that: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 + 6[H] \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ In practice you write the reagents as $\text{Sn}$ and $\text{HCl}$, with concentrated $\text{HCl}$ heated under reflux to drive the reaction to completion.

Final answer: organic compound: nitrobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$
reagents: $\text{Sn}$ and $\text{HCl}$
conditions: concentrated $\text{HCl}$ and heat / boil / reflux

hints: Count the carbons in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and think which functional groups already contain that same three carbon skeleton plus nitrogen.
Recall which powerful hydride reagent reduces both $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ and $\text{C=O}$ in $\text{CONH}_2$ down to $\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Find a three carbon precursor that already contains N**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ has three carbons and one nitrogen. Two neat options keep that skeleton: an amide, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$, where carbon is already attached to N, or a nitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, where carbon is triply bonded to N. Both can be reduced to the primary amine.

Pick the hydride donor that attacks C=O and C triple bond N**
$\text{NaBH}_4$ is too mild for these groups. Lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_4$, is the strong nucleophilic hydride source that delivers $\text{H}^-$ to the carbonyl carbon of the amide or the nitrile carbon: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CN} + 4[H] \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$$ $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2 + 4[H] \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ So state $\text{LiAlH}_4$ as the reagent.

Final answer: organic compound: propanamide, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$ OR propanenitrile, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CN}$
reagent: $\text{LiAlH}_4$

hints: Remember how an aromatic amine with a strongly activating $\text{NH}_2$ group behaves with bromine water compared with an aliphatic amine.
Think about the positions on the benzene ring where substitution occurs when the $\text{NH}_2$ group directs incoming electrophiles, and what colour the organic product is.
walkthrough:
Use the very different reactivity toward bromine**
The $\text{NH}_2$ group strongly activates the benzene ring in phenylamine, so electrophilic substitution is extremely fast even without a catalyst. Propylamine has no ring, so it cannot do this. Adding bromine water, $\text{Br}_2$(aq), therefore gives a white precipitate only with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, while the brown bromine colour simply fades with no precipitate for the aliphatic amine.

Draw the tribromo product**
Three $\text{Br}$ atoms substitute at the 2, 4 and 6 positions relative to the $\text{NH}_2$ group, which are the ortho and para positions: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + 3\text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_3\text{NH}_2 + 3\text{HBr}$$ Sketch a benzene ring, keep $\text{NH}_2$ at the top, then place $\text{Br}$ at both positions next to it and at the position directly opposite it. That molecule is 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine, seen as the white solid.

Final answer: testing reagent: bromine (aq) / $\text{Br}_2$(aq)
amine that gives a precipitate: phenylamine, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$
structure of precipitate: 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine, benzene ring with $\text{NH}_2$ at position 1 and $\text{Br}$ at positions 2, 4 and 6

hints: Start from the definition of a base as a proton acceptor and ask what feature on nitrogen allows $\text{NH}_3$ and amines to accept $\text{H}^+$.
Compare the environment of the nitrogen lone pair in phenylamine, where it sits next to a benzene pi system, with that in ammonia.
Consider how a propyl alkyl chain pushes electron density toward nitrogen compared with just hydrogen atoms in ammonia.
Put the three compounds in order by asking which lone pair is least available and which is most available for bonding to $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Link basicity to the nitrogen lone pair**
Basicity here means willingness to pick up $\text{H}^+$: $$\text{RNH}_2 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{RNH}_3^+$$ All three species, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{NH}_3$, have a lone pair on nitrogen. The more available that lone pair is to form a new N to H bond, the stronger the base.

See why phenylamine is the weakest**
In phenylamine the p orbital on nitrogen overlaps with the pi system of the ring. The lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring. Because it is partly pulled away from nitrogen, it is much less ready to accept $\text{H}^+$. That makes phenylamine a weaker base than ammonia.

See why propylamine is the strongest**
In propylamine the propyl group, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$, is electron donating by the inductive effect. It pushes electron density onto nitrogen, increasing the negative character around N and making the lone pair more attractive to $\text{H}^+$. Ammonia has only H atoms and no such donation, so propylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.

Write the final order**
Putting availability together: least available lone pair in phenylamine, intermediate in ammonia, most available in propylamine. Hence: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < \text{NH}_3 < \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$$ from least basic to most basic.

Final answer: phenylamine < ammonia < propylamine (least basic to most basic)
A base has a lone pair that can accept a proton / $\text{H}^+$.
In phenylamine the lone pair on N is delocalised into the benzene ring / pi-system, so less available.
In propylamine the alkyl group is electron donating, increasing electron density on N, so more available.
